content.text:
For a **common cold**, there’s no medicine that cures it—most colds get better on their own in about **7–10 days**, though cough can last longer. Medicines can help **relieve symptoms**. Antibiotics **don’t help** a cold because colds are caused by viruses. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**For adults, choose based on symptoms:**

- **Fever, headache, body aches, sore throat:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** can help. Follow the label, and avoid doubling up—many “multi-symptom” cold products already contain acetaminophen. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20351611?lt=&p=1&utm_source=openai))

- **Stuffy nose:**  
  Try **saline nasal spray/rinse**, steam, or a humidifier. A decongestant like **pseudoephedrine** may help, but ask a pharmacist/doctor first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems**, or take stimulants/MAOIs. Nasal decongestant sprays like oxymetazoline should generally be used **no more than 3 days** to avoid rebound congestion.

- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  An antihistamine may help, but some cause drowsiness.

- **Cough:**  
  **Honey** can help calm cough in adults and children over 1 year. A cough suppressant such as **dextromethorphan** may help a dry, irritating cough; **guaifenesin** may help loosen mucus. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

- **Sore throat:**  
  Lozenges/cough drops, warm fluids, and pain relievers can help. Don’t give lozenges to children under 4. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Avoid/ask first if:** you’re pregnant, have chronic medical conditions, take prescription meds, are treating a child, or have liver/kidney disease, ulcers/bleeding risk, or high blood pressure.

**Get medical advice urgently** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, dehydration, confusion, symptoms that get much worse, a fever that is high or persistent, or if you’re at high risk and symptoms could be **flu or COVID-19**—antiviral treatments work best early. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))
